    I actually bought this camcorder way back in 2016 but never got around to reviewing it. I only kept it for about a year before selling it to a pro. I liked almost everything about it, especially its looks - Beautiful!!

    But, alas, it was just a little too big for me. I'm just a retired guy who's always loved camcorders and have had tons of them. I'll always think very fondly of this beautiful machine but the Sony FDR-AX700 is a better fit for me and still performs really well. If I was a pro and still working, I would probably still have this beautiful machine. Four years later and I still miss it but at least I got a few hours of video that I made on it that I can watch and reminisce.

  • Amazon Customer
    5 out of 5 stars
    absolute workhorse
    Reviewed in Canada on December 23, 2019
    Verified Purchase
    Brief content visible, double tap to read full content.
    Full content visible, double tap to read brief content.

    This beast has been nothing but great for my video business. It's been a few years since it was my A-cam, now it's not even C-cam, but only because this workhorse took my business above and beyond, allowing me to level up my camera gear to much higher end cinema cameras like Red. That being said, we still use it for corporate type shoots, run and gun street jobs, and things of this nature. It shines really well in sports bringing 4k60p to your client that generally can't be achieved so easily. Great for clients with lower end budgets that don't warrant the big Hollywood cams. It feels good in your hands and on your shoulder, has excellent stabilization and zoom, great audio control, looks very professional. Image is quite good if exposed properly. It suffers in low light, but this isn't the right tool for low light jobs. Overall, for true camcorders under $15k this is the top camera.

  • Vlad H
    5 out of 5 stars
    Heavy, but well worth the effort. Updated on June 21, 2018.
    Reviewed in the United States on November 4, 2017
    Verified Purchase
    Brief content visible, double tap to read full content.
    Full content visible, double tap to read brief content.

    Very low noise with right settings, no chromatic aberration even when filming tree branches against the bright sky on tightest zoom, great image stabilization, good focusing aids. The lens is truly great and is a great find for travel shooter who can't possibly be swapping glass while being sprayed on the ship in the middle of the ocean. Its controls are numerous and features are countless, but investing in learning them pays off handsomely.

    June 2018 UPDATE after 9 months of usage.

    TL;DR: great camera, get it and enjoy it. Now the details.

    First, it's important to understand our perspective: my wife and I are are non-professional, hard-ish-core hobbyist travel photographers/videographers. We don't do interviews or weddings - instead it's mostly whales and glaciers. So our primary use case is "running and gunning"; not quite war-zone style, but we mostly shoot in adverse conditions, on ships, rubber boats, or shores where we have very limited time and thus we can't even think of setting up lights, etc. Our travel run-n-gun use case is why we got a fixed-lens camcorder. Also, my opinion is informed by coming from the full-frame DSLR background, where life is so much easier due to the large margin of error, with tons of detail recoverable in post-production.

    The notes below are not "cons" per se, but rather lessons learned and suggestions for Panasonic regarding possible future improvements, if they want to address concerns pertaining primarily to the run-n-gun workflow.

    1. Exposure.

    Dear DSLR shooter folks, if you read this, video is an order of magnitude more difficult in terms of how much (little) detail can be recovered in post. Even with 4/3 sensor and an amazing lens this camera has, and even if you shoot recording 10-bit 4:2:2 on Atomos with low-compression Avid or ProRes codec, if your exposure is off by one f-stop, the amount of loss in highlights or shadows respectively is pretty staggering. Exposing exactly correctly is crucial and here are what we learned and noted for this camcorder.

    - Follow the ND filter direction that camera gives, unless you are absolutely 100% sure the camera is wrong (it is wrong sometimes). Overexposing due to not paying attention to the ND filter recommendation was the largest source of issues for us so far. *Highlights going mad is probably the most difficult issue we have to deal with in this camera.* Having sky in a high-dynamic range scene has become a dreadful proposition, because not exposing exactly right leads to very irksome greenish-magenta tones in the highlights, making sky look quite bad, requiring bending over backwards later in DaVinci Resolve in order to mitigate the problem.

    - Use Waverform before every shot. Sometimes easier said than done, because if you use manual focus assist, you should turn that off first before waveform could be turned on. I think WF button should at least show the WF when it's being held down, regardless what else is on the screen. Another very odd thing is that is appears that WF can be only displayed on the LCD screen, but not in the viewfinder. Given that this camera's LCD has pretty mediocre brightness, not having such a critical exposure aid as WF in the viewfinder is really annoying and hard to justify. Atomos monitor/recorder, if you can afford one and don't mind lugging it around, mitigates this issue well, as it's very bright and can display WF before and during the recording.

    - Exposure compensation. (Oh how I miss my DLSR's exposure compensation dial!) Again, in our case, when you are tracking a flying albatross, it will go from backlit to frontlit, while the sky changes from sunny to overcast in a single shot, so forget the fully manual exposure. The only way we could figure out to how do the on-the-fly exposure comp is to put Backlit and Spotlight modes on user buttons. We have come to rely heavily on those crude, one-size-fits-all changes of exposure. If there was only one thing I could request to add to this camera's set of controls, is a dedicated exposure compensation dial.

    - Dynamic range. Even with all the modern magic and wizardry, images/footage produced by camcorders in this price range have very little DR compared to a full-frame DSLR. Therefore, managing DR settings carefully pays high dividend. Using Dynamic Range Stretch (DRS) and Log makes fair amount of difference. I keep DRS on as a default, because camcorders have high-contrast bias, so forgetting to turn DRS off is a lesser evil. DRS toggle is on the "speed-dial" too (meaning on the assignable user button). Re: Log, switching to VLog-L mode helps somewhat as it adds about 1.5 f-stops to the dynamic range. However, switching to Log mode does not seem to be made possible via a user button. With Log mode being not easily accessible, DRS is our the standard fallback. I'd like to be able to toggle Log mode via user button.

    - VLog-L. It's a great feature for reducing contrast and adding a stop or two to the dynamic range. However, for us, a great limiting factor for using Log mode is that the efficiency of focus assist drops to almost nothing in Log mode. Auto focus in this camera is contrast-based. When recording, this camcorder does not have enough computing power to translate low-contrast picture of Log to high-contrast Rec709 (regular, non-Log contrast), and thus prevents the camera from having enough contrast to perform either decent auto-focus, or provide reasonable manual focus assist. Log view assist, translating Log to Rec works only before recording starts, so focusing in Log is relatively easy only before you start rolling. Once record button is pushed, if your eyesight is not perfect or your eyes are simply tired, focusing in Log mode in run-n-gun situation is just too difficult to make Log a quick go-to mode for high-contrast scenes. Too often we have to fall back on DRS. Again, an external Atomos monitor is perfectly capable of translating Log to Rec in real time, providing great focus peaking aid at the same time, giving you great fighting chance to have both improved DR of Log and good focus at the same time, at the expense of extra dollars, weight, and an item to manage. Still, even with Log mode on, don't even think of having any exposure margin of error - you don't have it. Your highlights will go bonkers even in Log if you don't give your exposure and DR settings great amount of TLC :-).

    2. White Balance

    Second most-consequential error we make somewhat frequently is not tuning WB often enough. In good lighting conditions Auto WB does very respectable job. However, when it gets a little darker, or just overcast, the auto WB seems to get heavy cold tone bias, and setting WB manually against the white target card becomes essential - something that needs to be done every few minutes during the sunset in the evening or whenever lighting conditions are going through rapid transition.

    3. Focusing.

    Contrast-based auto-focus and manual focus aids are are not great. It means that with low-contrast scenes, on when Log mode is on, you are on your own with your probably imperfect eyesight. It seems that alternative, much-improved focusing technologies have matured quite some time ago, and the next iteration of the camera absolutely should have something better than this.

    4. Miscellaneous.

    LCD screen. For the cost of the camera, the not-that-bright LCD is a surprising place to cut product cost. Given that Waveform monitor - a crucial exposure aid - can be displayed only on the LCD screen, and that primary use case for a fixed lens camera is run-n-gun, combining these together means that LCD should be super-bright. That's something that needs to be addressed too. Again, 1000-nits bright Atomos monitor is a mitigator, if you can deal with managing it.

    - No 60fps in UHD HDR10 mode. When outputting 10-bit color, 4:2:2 gamma UHD signal to an external monitor/recorder, this camera can stream only 30 fps. That's not to knock it down - that's in the specs, but it makes this camera just a bit short of the holy-grail feature set. I'd happily take 10-bit 4:2:0 60 fps (if that's even possible) over 4:2:2 30 fps.

    - Sturdiness. It's OK. My lovely wife, who's the main camera person using this camcorder, once slipped and fell on an icy road in the permanent dark of the northern Norway winter, while having the camera in the moderately-padded backpack. The hood with a part of the front lens assembly was ripped out. The front of the lens is attached by about six tiny screw, screwed into plastic. The hit resulted in all screw holes losing thread. I was able to repair the damage myself by temporarily taping thing together, and later filling screw wholes with epoxy, attaching the front of the lens back as well as it was before. That was the only damage after that hard a hit, and it is a pretty good testament to the build quality of the camera. Still, somewhat expensive Orca-9 bag was in order to push our luck any further.

    - A wish, and a feature request: next gen of this camcorder should hopefully have enough computing power to compress 60-fps UHD HDR10 (10-bit, 4:2:2) footage to the regular U3 SD card using HEVC/H.265 codec. GoPro 6 black can pack 60-fps UHD 8-bit 4:2:0 using HEVC today, so given DVX200 large size, bigger battery and higher price, its successor should be the first affordable complete HDR10 system.

    - A note designers. Please consider that people using this camcorder are not all large dudes. A petite woman in our little family does significantly better camera job than a moderately tall man :-). Shorter distances between controls and reduced weight and size would be so great for smaller hands.

    Overall, this is a very-very good camcorder. Pretty much as good as it gets in this price range. Getting your exposure precisely right is the most crucial task when using it, and it is also pretty laborsome. We do recommend the camera very enthusiastically, but the workload of getting your footage right is somewhat heavy. Most of the shortcomings this camcorder has could be addressed by using an external Atomos Ninja Inferno monitor, which carries an additional cost in money, mobility and extra work associated with an additional device.

    I hope this is helpful.

    Full content visible, double tap to read brief content.

    I will admit that there was a period of about 3 months where I had decided that I hated this camera. Our production company uses a variety of cameras and up until we purchased the DVX200 we were about a 50/50 split in use between the Panasonic GH4 and the Panasonic HC-X1000. The GH4 produces great looking footage and is nearly impossible to beat in an interview setting. The HC-X1000 was the easier camera to use and provided much better stability but the smaller sensor meant that the footage had a tendency to be a bit noisy. .While both cameras shot in 4k it doesn't take long to realize that resolution is only a piece of the overall production. In fact, in my opinion, most cameras have a resolution that far exceeds the sensor that they are using (the HC-X1000 is an example, but the most notorious example are the GoPros).

    So enter the Panasonic AG-DVX200. It promised the run-and-gun flexibility of the HC-x1000 PLUS the same MFT sensor (size) of the GH4! Holy Toledo - that is a homerun!

    But it didn't start out that way.

    One of the great things about the DVX200 is it great flexibility in controls. You have two or three times the control options that you have with the HC-X1000. This is a good thing - as long as you invest the time in REALLY learning the camera. As for me.... I decided to start using it ASAP (hey it was a sizable investment!) and my original footage was far below my GH4 and the HC-X1000! I had a terrible time trying to focus on things near to the lens (Which changed when I realize that the camera actually has a Macro mode). I struggled with brightness, color, and sound. At one point I literally put the camera in my closet with the expectation that I was going to sell it.

    Then I decided to spend 3 or 4 hours and really try to understand how to set up the camera ....

    Now - I love it! Here is a run down.

    - Size - it is pretty darn big. Probably 2x larger than the HC-X1000. In fact, this is probably the biggest issue with the camera. I am struggling to find an appropriate sized case that will hold he camera that can still be used as my carry on luggage for flying.

    - Video Quality - When properly set-up it is very good. It definitely rivals my GH4 for sharpness and color. The larger sensor size means that it record in 4K with very little noise (much better than the HC-X1000). The quality does fade when you film 4k at 60FPS. The camera writes at 150MPS.... which probably isn't adequate. However, (I may be wrong) this is the absolute fastest write speed available on a (high end) SD card. I am curious to see the footage at 4K 60FPS when recorded on an external recorder.

    - Image stabilzation.... very, very good. In fact, I have shot footage inside a bounce house. Somehow the DVX-200 managed to capture the "bounce" without produce a noticeable abrupt shake.

    - Sound - I am still working on this one. The onboard mic is front point and directional. I have had difficulty finding a sweet spot for recording level/gain. I have now switched to using the Sennheiser MKE 600 with improving results. The DVX-200 has two XLR jacks that can supply 48V phantom power (same with HC-X1000x ... this differs from the GH4 which requires an add on to become XLR capable)

    - Zoom - very smooth with the ability to adjust two separate zooms to your need for speed.

    - Lens... pretty darn good. With some knowledge and practice you are able to get a shallower depth of field. Again, you will need a bit of knowledge on how to lock in your f-stop while adjusting the gain and shutter speed, but it can be done.

    -2 memory card slots

    -Capable to write in 4.2.2 but you will need an external recorder (like the one made by Atmos). I am really anxious to try recording in 4.2.2 to see if they will further improve the 4k footage.

    - Weight - not especially light or tripod friendly. The bottom of the camera is rather large which make it tough to work correctly with tripod slider plates. I am using a Manfrotto 504 and it requires the perfect placement in order to make it work.

    - Capability - can write at speeds up to 150m - which (obviously) requires a very fast SD card. The camera ill capture 4K at 60fps... just be ready for some very large files!

    Final Verdict - While the learning curve is rather steep - the DVX200 seems to be a combination of the best of both the GH4 and the HC-X1000. The camera costs about 50% more than the HC-X1000 so it isn't necessarily a slam dunk option. However, if you are looking for cleaner footage at 4k (when you start dropping down to 1080 I think the advantage diminishes) the DVX200 probably warrants the difference in price. Compared to the GH4.... the DVX200 provides much better image stability and dual XLR inputs, at a much higher price and size (the GH4 is like an iphone when compared to this thing!). Also, with the proper lens you can get a much shallower DoF on the GH4. However, for me... the DVx200 is the best camera for the job for about 80% of my video needs. In order to get another improvement in performance you will likely need to spend 3 or 4x over the cost of the DVX200.

    4 1/2 Stars
